newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Is Hong Kong return a glimpse of Taiwan's future?.
newsitem.headline: Is Hong Kong return a glimpse of Taiwan's future?.

text.p: "One country, two systems". If the model can work to graft an unabashedly capitalist Hong Kong onto a communist-ruled China, can it work for exuberantly democratic and anti-communist Taiwan as well?
For Beijing, the answer is yes. Taiwan adamantly disagrees.

The cold reality of Hong Kong's final push toward Chinese sovereignty is forcing a reluctant Taiwan to take a hard look at what Beijing insists is a rosy vision of the estranged island's "return to the motherland".

Hong Kong's pace toward reunification with China after 150 years as a British colony quickened on Wednesday with the Beijing-orchestrated selection of shipping mogul Tung Chee-hwa to take the territorial reins as chief executive on July 1.

Through 1996, Chinese officials laying the groundwork for the takeover have said the process should reassure Taiwan that Beijing is earnest in its pledge to allow the island to keep its political system after reunifying with the mainland.

"We must let Taiwan compatriots see that the principle of one country, two systems is feasible and also in the interests of all the Chinese people, including Taiwan compatriots," Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who is overseeing the handover for Beijing, said in March.

Qian quoted paramount leader Deng Xiaoping -- who in 1984 got British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher to accept the concept for Hong Kong -- as saying Taiwan would have even greater freedoms under one country, two systems.
"The policies toward the Taiwan question are more lenient than those for the Hong Kong issue," Qian said in a reference to Deng's vow to let Taiwan keep its powerful armed forces.
Taiwan's Republic of China government, deeply suspicious of Beijing since losing a civil war to the communists in 1949 and taking refuge on the island, rejects the idea outright.

"It's absolutely impossible for us to accept communist China's so-called theory of one country, two systems," President Lee Teng-hui, the first popularly elected president in Chinese history, said in July.
"The Republic of China is different from Hong Kong."

One big difference is that Taiwan has long had full economic and political autonomy and has built democracy actively since 1987, when the Nationalist government lifted martial law imposed in part to ensure security against mainland infiltrators.
Political leaders and analysts say there is widespread doubt on Taiwan that Beijing can keep its hands-off promise.
"China will not be able to keep its hands off Hong Kong like it said it would," said Hsu Hsin-liang, head of Taiwan's main opposition Democratic Progressive Party.

"The whole world is watching with interest how much a so-called 'autonomous' region without sovereignty can be autonomous," Hsu said, referring to Hong Kong's future status as a "special autonomous region" of China.

Political analyst Tim Ting said the most optimistic scenario was one in which China itself embraced democratic reforms over the next decade, something that would hinge on whether President and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin consolidates his power.

"What's a potential trouble is that if Mr Jiang loses power in China, and the line of power from Deng Xiaoping to Jiang Zemin is disrupted, we cannot predict what will happen to the promise of one country, two systems," Ting said.
Such a disruption in Beijing "could affect the Taiwanese people's support of one country, two systems", Ting said.

Ting said Beijing was unlikely to take "severe measures" against Taiwan before 2000 despite its standing vow to retake the island by force if it seeks independence and its menacing war games in the months before Taiwan's presidential poll.
But after sovereignty over Hong Kong and later Macau in 1999 is assured, China's growing economic and military clout all but guarantees that Beijing's pressure on Taiwan will mount.
Local media said all Taiwanese eyes would be on Hong Kong.
"If Hong Kong's democracy goes backward after 1997, how can communist China expect Taiwan to have confidence in reunification?" the China Times said in an editorial.
"Communist China therefore should exercise self control and avoid excessive intervention in Hong Kong affairs," it said.
